A.explanation: Combined velocity $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $h = v^2/(2g) \approx 5.1\text{ m}$.

B.explanation: Uses only $95\text{ g}$ as the moving mass after impact, giving $v \approx 10.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $h \approx 5.6\text{ m}$.

C.explanation: Omits the factor of $1/2$ in kinetic energy, using $v^2 = gh$ instead of $v^2 = 2gh$ to get about $10\text{ m}$.

D.explanation: Equates initial pellet kinetic energy directly to $mgh$, ignoring kinetic energy lost in the perfectly inelastic embedding.

hints: Notice the $5.0\text{ g}$ pellet at $200\text{ m s}^{-1}$ sticks in the stationary $95\text{ g}$ block, so first find their common velocity just after impact.
Apply conservation of linear momentum with total mass $5.0 + 95 = 100\text{ g}$ because the collision is perfectly inelastic.
Convert the post-impact kinetic energy of the $100\text{ g}$ combined mass into gravitational potential energy $mgh$ to find the rise $h$.
walkthrough: The impact is perfectly inelastic because the $5.0\text{ g}$ pellet embeds in the $95\text{ g}$ block, so momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
Use $m_{p}u = (m_{p}+m_{b})v$ with $m_{p} = 0.0050\text{ kg}$, $m_{b} = 0.095\text{ kg}$ and $u = 200\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Substitute: $0.0050 \times 200 = 0.100 \times v$, so $v = 1.0/0.100 = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ just after impact.
For the free rise, kinetic energy becomes potential energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh$, so $h = v^2/(2g)$.
Substitute $v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$: $h = 100/(2 \times 9.81) \approx 5.1\text{ m}$. This is option A.
